newsitem.title: KENYA: Australian tells of hard ordeal in Somali jail.
newsitem.headline: Australian tells of hard ordeal in Somali jail.

text.p: An Australian pilot freed after 131 days in a Somali jail said on Saturday he was held short of water in a tiny, windowless cell for up to 22 hours a day.

Justin Fraser, 24, was freed in the southwestern town of Baidoa on Thursday and flown to Nairobi after Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi intervened and asked faction leader Hussein Aideed, who heads a self-declared government, to release him.
"I was locked in a room approximately the size of a shipping crate, a windowless room. I had nothing," Fraser told a Nairobi news conference, adding he only got a blanket after two weeks.
"It was difficult, very hard...After a few days they gave me a plastic sleeping mat...and that was it. Generally speaking I was locked in for 21, 22 hours a day," the Australian said.

"When you're in there, it's very hard because you're dying of thirst, you're really thirsty, and they won't give you a water bottle and you can't drink too much when you are outside because you have nothing (inside) to use as a toilet," he said.
Fraser, pale, thin and still shocked, then stopped for a few minutes to pull himself together. His mother, Pauline Dickson who campaigned for his release, left the room in tears.

He lost 16 kg (35 pounds) in 131 days in captivity after being forced by mechanical problems to land his plane in the western Somali town of Huddur after flying in a load of qat, a mild narcotic plant chewed by Somalis and grown in Kenya.
Fraser was sentenced to 25 years in jail for flying without clearance and entering Somalia without an Aideed government visa despite visas not being required for pilots in transit.

He said he believed the main reason for his bad treatement was because he was victimised by a deputy attorney-general of the government led by Mohamed Farah Aideed, Hussein's father who died on August 1. He later heard the official was fired.
He said the official, known as Ahmed "Food", apparently "had a problem with white people" as he had been punished by Italians when they occupied south Somalia before independence.
"He saw his opportunity (with me) to get even," he said.
"I didn't feel I had done anything to deserve being treated like this," said the Australian, adding he was even not allowed to take back some of his own money to buy soap and a blanket.
He said from sleeping on the floor he had developed a bad chest infection and head cold and was constantly worried about catching malaria, which may have been fatal in his condition.
Fraser said after about four weeks the door was opened during the daytime and he was allowed to move around in the compound but was not allowed to speak to any of the other prisoners.
A general in charge of the region told him the government had made a mistake and he was being held for saying bad things about it and his company was not allowed to fly in Somalia.
He said he then wrote a letter to the provincial chief, asking when he was going to be charged as a political prisoner and offering to pay his 600,000 Somali shilling fine ($75,000).
"After I wrote the letter, I was locked back into the room and remained there," said Fraser, adding that only after his mother visited him was the cell door left open during the day.
He said his guards wielding walking sticks hit him twice when he protested about his imprisonment and banged and kicked on the cell door so much he cut his wrist and hurt his ankle.
He said when he argued that he had flown into Somalia 200 times before he was told he should have approached the first Somali he saw and asked for permission to be in his country.

He praised the prison commander for giving him newspaper articles but said unfortunately he brought the same one three times. In a rare moment of humour at the news conference, Fraser added however he had found it interesting every time.
